fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "The Energetic Architecture Model", "body": "Popham describes a model he calls energetic architecture, built on the Universal patterns he finds repeating across traditional systems. He points to the elements of earth, fire, water, air and ether, noting that Chinese thought substitutes metal and wood, and to the threefold divisions everywhere: the tridosha of Ayurveda, the three treasures and the dantian of Chinese medicine, the cardinal, fixed and mutable modes of astrology, and alchemy's three philosophical principles of sulfur, mercury and salt. From the Prima Materia through duality to the elements, he argues, the same archetypal pattern is macrocosmic and microcosmic, present in every person and every plant in differing ratios."}, {"title": "Gnosis Cardiaca: Knowledge Through The Heart", "body": "Garton reads a passage from the book on gnosis cardiaca, and Popham credits the idea largely to the late Stephen Harrod Buhner and his book The Secret Teachings of Plants, acknowledging that the science in it has come under scrutiny. The premise, as Popham relays it, is that everything emanates an electromagnetic frequency carrying information, and that the human heart is the body's greatest oscillator, able to entrain with other fields. He uses a radio dial as the analogy: you tune past static until the fields synchronize. He is candid that it is also easy to mistake your own thoughts for something received."}, {"title": "Why He Calls It Evolutionary Herbalism", "body": "Popham argues Western herbalism has lurched through identity crises while Chinese medicine, Ayurveda, Tibetan medicine, Kampo and Unani Tibb held continuity for centuries. His evolutionary model deliberately layers those stages rather than choosing between them: folk and bioregional practice where people learned from the plants themselves, the vitalist and energetic systems reading hot, cold, wet and dry, and the modern biomedical work on plant chemistry and double blind placebo controlled studies. Science has a lot to offer, he says, but he does not think we should abandon tradition for its sake. He names his contribution as reviving Western alchemy and medical astrology, once mainstream in the Renaissance."}, {"title": "Treating The Person, Not The Disease", "body": "Asked how his holistic evaluation works, Popham frames a symptom as a language, a communication that something deeper is off, and contrasts that with what he calls allopathic herbalism, the use this herb for that symptom mindset. He describes constitutional or tissue state assessment across three variables: temperature, moisture, and the tonal quality of the tissue. Beyond that he wants the whole timeline of a person's life, home, family and food, sometimes taking over two hours for an initial consultation, alongside tools like pulse and tongue reading, blood work and, for him, medical astrology. A teacher's line stuck with him: reaching first for an herb misses the point entirely."}, {"title": "Poison Into Medicine As Inner Alchemy", "body": "The conversation turns toward reframing. Popham holds that everyone carries trauma to varying degrees and that healing means refusing the role of constant victim, reorienting perception so the experience teaches something and turns weakness into strength. He connects this to what he calls the practical premise of laboratory alchemy, poison into medicine, applied inwardly. His final step in evaluation is to ask which archetypal forces, elemental or planetary, are excessive or deficient in a person, and how to turn that force from its dark side toward its light side. Garton, who practices biofield tuning, ties it back to the healing power of simply being witnessed."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: The great Herbalism teacher Sajah Popham joins InnerVerse to discuss his book, Evolutionary Herbalism. In this conversation we explore Sajah's calling to plant medicine, the fractal wholeness of nature in each being, the alchemist's secret fire, gnosis of the heart, training intuition, plants as conscious beings, holistic evaluation for treating people instead of symptoms, and the healing achieved by reframing our identity-story.
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: In the Plus+ Extension you'll learn about the plant patterns taught by alchemy & astrology, how to connect the metaphysical to the material, the threefold pattern of nature, Mercury the savior & spiritual alchemy, the creation of the pure plant stone and its mysterious power, planetary signatures of plants, recognizing astrological signatures of plants, and tips on how to develop a personal relationship with the planets.

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Metaphysics Anchored in the Physical Plant", "body": "Sajah explains that an accurate metaphysical attribute of a plant or a person should never float apart from what is happening physically, which is why he was frustrated by herbal texts that listed physical actions in one column and emotional effects in another. For him the body is the most condensed part of the soul and the soul the most volatile part of the body. Chance adds his image of the mustard seed that becomes a tree, and Sajah shows how a planetary correlation, such as Mars in the serrated, stinging nettle rich in iron, describes habitat, shape, taste, organ affinity and inner virtue at once."}, {"title": "Sulfur, Mercury and Salt in Every Plant", "body": "The tria prima of alchemy names three archetypal principles: sulfur as the soul, mercury as the spirit, and salt as the body. Sajah maps them onto plant chemistry, with essential oils carrying the unique character of an herb, ethyl alcohol arising from any fermented plant as its universal spirit, and alkaline mineral salts left after repeated burning and grinding as its purified body. He notes that calling alcohol spirits comes straight from alchemy, and he values the soul and spirit distinction because it honors both our individuality and our universality, answering the new age refrain that we are all one."}, {"title": "Mercury the Savior and the Inner Work", "body": "Chance raises the idea that the solvent and the savior share a root, and suggests that spiritual growth means moving from an external savior story toward the realization that no one outside of you can save you. Sajah reads fermentation as the underworld journey of facing inner darkness, followed by distillation that exalts the spirit back up. He insists spagyrics is not merely putting ash back into a tincture but a whole cosmology and practice, and recalls a friend's advice to flip everything, since a finished remedy is only half the work until the plant takes the person through the same process."}, {"title": "The Plant Stone and Spagyric Chemistry", "body": "Sajah walks through volatile liquid preparations and fixed solid ones, from the quintessence built on four elements to the plant stone, made by imbibing salts with sulfur and mercury until they congeal. Legend says a lavender stone can pull the three principles out of a bucket of lavender water, though he has never seen it. Works are timed to the ruling planet, so rose, ruled by Venus, can stir Venusian synchronicities. He also describes tincturing an herb in alcohol fermented from that same plant, and a chemist's analysis showing that recombined salts and tincture form compounds absent from either part alone."}, {"title": "Building a Relationship With the Planets", "body": "Following his teacher Judith Hill, Sajah uses tropical astrology for medical work, explaining that a sign marks a season rather than a constellation, and he borrows the idea of six pairs of opposites for southern hemisphere students. Asked whether people can relate to the planets as they do to plants, he says the planets represent facets of the psyche and suggests tracking planetary hours, recalling coffee shop shifts where Mars hours brought accidents and Mercury hours brought chatty customers. He also recommends a moon journal, while Chance cautions against squeezing every drop from astrology and shares how he and his wife watch their lunar returns."}]
